title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-22
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-22 of the hermes-consultant series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson about estimation, what is the central focus?
options: A history of project management software
A review of unrelated scheduling tools
A summary of finance policy
Estimation as a sizing decision that produces a task you can start, complete, and verify in one focused window
questions.explanation: The lesson reframes estimation from predicting the future to deciding how you will work right now, optimizing for a shape of work you can actually complete.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Large tasks are easier to report because they produce one moment of completion
A small task is reportable because honesty depends on knowing what actually happened, which is easier at small scale
A task that needs research and building is fine as a single piece of work
Slice work by activity, write the tests then the code then the docs
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a small task is finishable, verifiable, reportable, and has bounded failure, which is why it ships reliably.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Order the slices by convenience so the easy work happens first
A task that needs a reviewer to trust it is a sign to power through without review
Split a big goal by deliverable, apply a window test to each slice, and order the slices risk-first
One large task is better than ten small ones because it produces momentum
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches to split by deliverable, apply the 30 to 45 minute window test to each slice, and put the uncertain part first so its failure is cheap.

questions.question: Per the lesson about packaging reusable skills, what is the central focus?
options: Capturing what you built as a reusable skill written to travel to the next client without leaking the last one
A tutorial on documentation tools
A review of unrelated project software
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the discipline of turning the reusable core of a solved problem into an asset that makes the next delivery cheaper and lower risk.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Write the skill at the end of the engagement from memory to capture the final state
The description is the trigger, so name the situation it applies to, not just the topic
Skills should hold incident narration and ticket numbers so the next person understands the story
Any procedure that worked once, however trivial, deserves a skill
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the description is the only part loaded when deciding relevance, so it must name the situation the skill applies to.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Client specifics belong in the skill so it travels with all the details
Credentials belong in the skill file so the environment stays shareable
Never put a credential in a skill file, parameterize paths, and scrub client names so the asset stays shareable
A skill with no pitfall is the most valuable kind
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches to strip the client out: no credentials in the file, parameterize settings, and scrub names so the skill is a reusable asset, not a liability.

questions.question: Per the lesson about documentation and handover, what is the central focus?
options: Making the client self-sufficient by naming an owner, building three document types, testing them live, and moving ownership
A tutorial on wiki software
A review of unrelated chat tools
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a handover is the transfer of ownership and operating knowledge so the client can run, maintain, and change the system without you.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: The reproduce doc is the one the client opens at two in the morning
A presentation that narrates your work proves the client can operate it
The runbook is the operate doc that gets opened in an emergency, and the evolve doc makes the client genuinely independent
Write all documentation from memory on the last day so it reflects the final system
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the runbook is what gets opened when the report does not land, and the evolve doc is what makes the client truly independent.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A system that runs on your personal API key is fine if it is well documented
The handover is verified when a competent client team member runs the system using only the documents and does not ask you a question
Secrets belong in the documentation so the client knows the values
Credentials should be transferred on the last day in a panic
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a handover is verified the same way a build is, once it survives a stranger using it without your help.

questions.question: Per the lesson about change management and adoption, what is the central focus?
options: A system nobody uses is a failed engagement; the craft of separating change from adoption and designing the agent around how people already work
A tutorial on marketing agent products
A review of unrelated time-tracking tools
A summary of payroll policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on closing the gap between delivering change and delivering adoption, which is where agent engagements quietly die.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Training harder fixes most adoption failures because they are caused by ignorance
The old spreadsheet is the incumbent and always wins on default until using the agent is easier in the way the user feels
Mandate from a manager is the most reliable way to spread adoption
Adoption is a mass-market problem best solved with company-wide announcements
questions.explanation: The lesson argues most adoption failures are a fit or trust problem, not ignorance, and the incumbent habit wins until the new way is better where the user feels it.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The owner and the champion are the same person with authority and credibility
Authority alone spreads a tool and is enough to drive adoption
Adoption is measured by the number of features shipped to the client
You need both an owner who can say we use this now and a champion whose painful problem the agent solves
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that authority unblocks while credibility spreads, so you need both an owner and a champion to make adoption stick.

questions.question: Per the lesson about governance and guardrails, what is the central focus?
options: A history of compliance software
A review of unrelated security tools
Writing an acceptable-use policy, treating PII as a bounded resource, and building guardrails that enforce the rules mechanically
A summary of marketing policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a capable, unattended agent needs governance as a design decision made up front, not a compliance checkbox.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A guardrail relies on the agent deciding to behave
Hold the minimum personal data the work needs and retrieve the rest on demand, keeping raw records out of persistent memory
Write the acceptable-use policy after the build so it describes what you already built
Copy customer data into an external memory provider without asking the client
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the safest personal data is the data that does not exist in your system, so you hold the minimum and retrieve on demand.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Auto-approving unattended work is a governance feature because it is convenient
Guardrails are unnecessary because the agent will stay in bounds
The write sandbox is optional and only limits convenience
In unattended cron work the default should be deny on dangerous commands so a scheduled agent is blocked rather than auto-approved
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the deny default for unattended work is a governance decision you should keep, so recurring agents cannot silently run destructive commands.

questions.question: Per the lesson about monitoring and observability, what is the central focus?
options: A history of monitoring dashboards
The craft of knowing when an agent is quietly failing, by separating loud from quiet failures and watching the whole fleet and the output
A review of unrelated logging tools
A summary of IT policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches observability as the ability to know what is happening inside a system from outside it, catching the failure no guardrail catches.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A loud failure is the worst kind because it makes the client nervous
Execution history alone proves the output was correct
A quiet failure is one that produces no error at all while the output is simply wrong
Stopping at it ran is enough because it is the important floor
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that quiet failures produce no error while being wrong, and are discovered by the client weeks in, which is the worst place.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A green dashboard is the same as observability
Checking only the star job is sufficient since the others rarely drift
Relying on memory to run the fleet check is reliable
Check the whole fleet on a schedule of your own, and sample the actual output because no status system can catch stale content
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that you check the whole fleet on your own schedule and sample the substance of output, because a status screen will not tell you the numbers are stale.

questions.question: Per the lesson about cost management, what is the central focus?
options: A history of billing software
A review of unrelated spreadsheet tools
Measuring unit cost, putting each piece of work on the right model tier, budgeting recurring load, and pricing the engagement from measurement
A summary of sales policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches how to make the number measured and turn a measured unit cost into a client number that survives the month.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Price the engagement from token math you have not observed
Leave every auxiliary task on auto so summarization runs on the premium model
A five-minute health check should run as an agent job for reliability
Measure a week of real runs before you put a number in a proposal, and never price from a demo
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that a three-run demo tells you nothing, so you measure a week of real runs before pricing.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Model choice is the largest cost difference in a long-running agent
The cache is the biggest cost lever because a mid-session model switch re-reads the whole context at full price
Switching models mid-conversation is always cheap
Inference is the largest cost of the engagement and should drive the price
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the cache is the biggest single lever, since a switch mid-conversation discards the cached prefix and re-reads the full context at full price.
